dataSetInformation.common:generalComment: The model uses only the official EF secondary data sets (plus a few approved proxies). The data set covers all materials along the supply chain of the represented cradle to gate inventory with a good overall data quality. The bill of materials is mainly based on the LOT 27 ErP preparatory study ENERG/C3/413-2010-LOT 27-Sli2.611335 with modification by the UPS Technical Secretariat. This data set is based on primary data from internationally adopted production processes, connected with regional precursor chains.

technology.technologyDescriptionAndIncludedProcesse: The main battery technology for existing UPS products is lead acid. This is a sealed, valve regulated lead acid battery. For the smaller sizes UPS products, the battery is often incorporated within the casing of the UPS. In terms of the bill of materials for lead acid batteries, recent research indicates that the following composition is typical: • Lead / Lead Oxides – 60% • Polypropylene – 10% • Sulphuric acid – 10% • Water – 16% • Glass – 2% • Antimony – 1.8% The initial process begins with the manufacturing of grids from an alloy of lead mixed with a small percentage of other metals. The grids conduct the current and provide a structure for the active material to hold. Next, a paste mixture of lead oxide - which is powdered lead and other materials - sulfuric acid and water is applied to the grids. Expander material made of powdered sulfates is added to the paste to produce negative plates. Such a pasted plate will need to be cured. Curing takes place in a controlled environment with warm to high temperatures and modifying humidity for two to four continuous days. During this process, the crystallization growth occurs which binds the paste to the grids. Once cured, the plates are required to completely cool and dry. Once the plates are ready, they will need to be alternatively stacked with a piece of separator between them. Separators are sheets of porous material that prevent short circuits, yet allow electrical current to flow between the plates. Once appropriately combined, all the positives are connected together, and separately, all the negatives are connected together. This combination of positives, negatives and separators combined is referred to as an element. The elements are then properly oriented and inserted into the battery case and welded together. Elements are arranged in series. Next, a cover is sealed to the top of the case, which contains the connected elements, and the terminal posts are formed outside creating an acid tight seal. Since the battery construction is now complete, it can be filled with sulfuric acid or electrolyte and placed onto the formation charge. During the formation charge, the battery is connected to an electrical source and charged for many hours. Finally, once a battery is fully formed, it will endure various quality checks and be cleaned and labelled before arriving at a location for sale.

LCIMethodAndAllocation.deviationsFromLCIMethodApproaches: Background system: For the combined heat and power production, allocation by exergetic content is applied. For the electricity generation and by-products, e.g. gypsum, allocation by market value is applied due to no common physical properties. Within the refinery allocation by net calorific value and mass is used. For the combined crude oil, natural gas and natural gas liquids production allocation by net calorific value is applied. For details please see the document "GaBi Databases Modelling Principles"
LCIMethodAndAllocation.modellingConstants: Carbon storage and delayed emissions: credits associated with temporary (carbon) storage or delayed emissions are not considered. Emissions off-setting: not included. Capital goods are included, unless exclusion is justified along the overall 1% cut-off criterion. Direct land use change: GHG emissions from direct LUC allocated to good/service for 20 years after the LUC occurs. Fossil and biogenic carbon emissions and removals: removals and emissions are modelled as follows: All GHG emissions from fossil fuels (including peat and limestone) are modelled consistently with the ILCD list of elementary flows. In the case that the emissions refer to the molecules CO2 and CH4, they are modelled as ‘carbon dioxide (fossil)’ and ‘methane (fossil)’. Biogenic uptake and emissions are not modelled separately. For land use change, all carbon emissions and uptakes are inventoried separately for each of the elementary flows. Soil carbon accumulation (uptake) via improved agricultural management is excluded from the model.

dataSourcesTreatmentAndRepresentativenes.dataCutOffAndCompletenessPrinciples: cover at least 95% of environmental impacts
dataSourcesTreatmentAndRepresentativenes.dataSelectionAndCombinationPrinciples: The model predominantly uses the mandatory EF data sets for both the foreground system and the background system, wherever available.
dataSourcesTreatmentAndRepresentativenes.useAdviceForDataSet: This LCI results data set is the (market) representative product of the lead acid battery, developed in context of the European Commission’s Environmental Footprint pilot phase 2013-2018. The datasets are specifically developed in compliance with the methodological requirements under the EF. The system boundary of this data set is cradle-to-gate.

common:scope.name: LCI results or Partly terminated system

review.common:reviewDetails: The data set achieves an overall DQR of 1.75, under the EF scheme of the PEFCR guidance 6.3. It meets the requirements for an EF compliant data set, as specified in the referenced documents of the compliant system, i.e. PEFCR guidance 6.3 Special remodelling instructions, and the applicable PEFCR. The foreground model is well representative of the depicted EU market of the reference flow, regarding both technological, geographical and time-related representativeness, while some relevant background data sets are less representative in these three aspects. The background data sets have moreover some limitations in terms of consistency, as they stem from different data providers without full consistency of the background system of those background data sets (aside from energy and transport data that are the same in foreground and across all background data); the use of these background data sets is however mandatory under the EF scheme. The completeness of elementary flows of the 15 EF impact categories is “good” for the foreground system and mostly “good” but often only “fair” for some parts of the background system. The LCIA result of the data set per reference flow is plausible. The data set documentation is appropriate in scope and detail, and correctly reflects the model (judged with samples), including meeting the permissible cut-off rules, LCI modelling provisions and (fully checked) system boundaries. Based on expert judgement, the uncertainty of the data set is sufficiently limited. The names, classes/categories of newly created flows and processes are ILCD compliant, otherwise exclusively the eligible ILCD reference elementary flows, flow properties and unit groups are being used, including the regionalisation of the large majority of the water and land use flow amounts.
